canberra.title: Bird flu detected in Goulburn, no signs of mass mortality says NSW Government
canberra.snippet: The H5 bird flu has now been detected in Goulburn alongside four other new regions across NSW, bringing the confirmed cases in the state ...
canberra.content:
11 September 2026

Start the conversation

A Greater Crested Tern on the South Coast. Photo: Karyn Starmer.

The H5 bird flu has now been detected in Goulburn alongside four other new regions across NSW, bringing the confirmed cases in the state up to 30.

The event in Goulburn has seen a Greater Crested Tern infected with the virus, with Dee Why and Hawks Nest also recording cases in the same species of bird.

Meanwhile, Moruya has recorded cases in Silver Gulls, and Congo has recorded cases in the White-fronted Tern.

The NSW Government is working closely with the poultry industry based in Goulburn to prevent the spread of the virus to poultry flocks of captive birds, while also remaining adamant that the risk to humans remains low.

Minister for Agriculture, Regional and Western NSW Tara Moriarty said the new detections were a reminder for people to remain vigilant and to remain on top of surveillance and reporting.

“We’re working closely with the poultry industry to reduce the risk of the virus spreading,” she said.

“NSW has recommended poultry owners voluntarily house birds, and the NSW poultry industry continues to operate normally.

“Now is the time for everyone who has backyard chickens or pet birds in aviaries to take precautionary steps to ensure there are no interactions between their chooks and pets and wild birds.”

Minister for the Environment Penny Sharpe reinforced the need to report sick birds, stating it is impossible to eradicate the disease once it establishes itself in the wild bird population.

“The NSW Government has commenced a rollout of targeted vaccinations for vulnerable species of birds to help protect them against H5 avian influenza,” she said.

“We are focused on strong surveillance, preparedness and practical measures that reduce the spread of H5 bird flu and help protect our most vulnerable native wildlife.

“If you see a sick or dead bird, please ensure you and your pets avoid contact. Record what you see on your phone and report it via the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline.”

The NSW Chief Veterinary Officer Dr Joanne Coombe said while the number of bird flu events was growing, there had been no signs of mass mortalities in NSW.

“A national surveillance plan is in operation to monitor for any further detections and facilitate rapid, coordinated response,” she said.

“If you see sick or dead wild birds, domestic birds, marine mammals or other wildlife showing signs of H5 bird flu, avoid contact, record what you see, report it via the online reporting form or contact the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.”

canberra.title: Quack on, Canberra! It’s time to sink your teeth into Floriade 2026!
canberra.snippet: More than a million flowers are about to bloom in Commonwealth Park, but this year one of Floriade’s more unusual creations might steal s...
canberra.content:
Visitors explore vibrant, blooming garden beds during the opening of Floriade 2026 at Commonwealth Park in Canberra. Pic: John Lomnicki.

More than a million flowers are about to bloom in Commonwealth Park, but this year one of Floriade’s more unusual creations might steal some of their attention.

It is big, floral and unmissable.

“Somewhere a very talented group of people looked at more than a million flowers and asked the question, what is the highest expression of horticultural excellence?” Chief Minister Andrew Barr joked during a preview of the festival.

“And the answer was a massive duck cake.

“And frankly, I respect this decision.”

Floriade opens on Saturday (12 September), beginning a month-long takeover of Commonwealth Park that will bring flowers, food, music, celebrity chefs and thousands of interstate visitors into the heart of Canberra.

This year’s theme, Feast of Flowers, links gardens with food, harvest and the traditions built around them.

It follows a record year. More than half a million people attended Floriade in 2025, the largest crowd in the festival’s history.

While the million-plus blooms remain the main attraction, organisers have leaned heavily into food this year.

Cook and food educator Stephanie Alexander will appear for a book talk, while chefs Karen Martini, Mindy Woods, Justine Schofield and Simon Bryant are among those taking part in demonstrations and appearances. Markets, workshops, entertainment and family activities will run throughout the festival.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr at the opening of the Floriade 2026. Photos: John Lomnicki.

Mr Barr said it was also an opportunity to show visitors how far Canberra’s food scene had moved from some of the stereotypes still attached to the capital.

“Our food scene has become one of Australia’s best-kept secrets,” he said.

“Well, actually, maybe it’s not really a secret anymore.”

He joked that when visitors expressed surprise at Canberra’s restaurants, he wondered, “In which century did you get that information from?”

“Some people seem to have formed a view of Canberra around the time they bought their last street directory.”

Beyond the food and floral displays, this year’s gardens include Aboriginal cultural experiences with Uncle Richie and Auntie Violet, featuring plants used for bush tucker and medicinal purposes, including species native to the Canberra region.

Head gardener Kira Buckley said visitors would also see new flower varieties mixed among familiar favourites, including different narcissus varieties and changes to the pansy displays.

And when daylight is no longer enough, Floriade will stay awake.

NightFest returns from 1 to 4 October, lighting up the gardens and bringing live music and after-dark entertainment to Commonwealth Park. The Temper Trap, Tim Finn, Pacific Avenue, Busby Marou and Christine Anu are among this year’s headline acts.

Mr Barr couldn’t resist playing with Canberra’s reputation for being quiet after hours.

NightFest, he said, provided “useful evidence that Canberrans do in fact leave the house after dark”.

“And it offers annual proof that our nightlife extends well beyond parliamentary sitting weeks.”

But behind the jokes is an event closely tied to Canberra’s identity.

Floriade began in 1988 and has grown alongside the city. Mr Barr said generations who were once brought to the festival by their parents were now returning with their own children.

“People come here with family, with friends, with visitors from interstate,” he said.

“People come because their parents brought them, and they’re now bringing their kids, and every year new traditions are created.”

The festival is also a significant tourism drawcard, bringing hundreds of thousands of people into Canberra and supporting hospitality and other local businesses.

Getting there, however, could require a little more planning this year.

Major construction is continuing around the city, with changed pedestrian and cycling access around Commonwealth Avenue.

Free daily Floriade shuttle buses will operate through the city and National Triangle, while weekend express services will run from Tuggeranong, Woden and Belconnen bus interchanges. Visitors are being encouraged to use public transport or check parking and changed access arrangements before leaving home.

Floriade runs from 12 September to 11 October, and general entry remains free.

And for anyone wondering what to wear while admiring a million spring flowers, Mr Barr offered perhaps the most reliably Canberra advice of the morning.

“If you’re wondering whether you’ll need a puffer jacket over the next month, the answer is: you are in Canberra in early spring; it is best to be prepared.”

The flowers may say spring. Canberra’s weather, as usual, reserves the right to disagree.

To find out more and plan your visit, go to Floriade Australia.

canberra.title: Coalition votes against online safety changes and flags intention to do the same over algorithms
canberra.snippet: Federal Government legislation to double fines for tech firms breaching the under-16s social media ban passed Parliament with the help of...
canberra.content:
11 September 2026

Join the conversation

3

Further amendments to the Online Safety Act have passed parliament. Now to the deal with Labor’s incoming Digital Duty of Care bill. Photo: Iconiq Visuals.

Federal Government legislation to double fines for tech firms breaching the under-16s social media ban passed Parliament with the help of the Greens and some independent senators, including the ACT’s David Pocock.

Maximum penalties for systematic breaches of the minimum age laws will jump from $49.5 million to $99 million for the tech giants, while individual executives refusing to comply could face fines up to $364,000 and jail terms of up to 12 months.

The amendment to the Online Safety Act also gives eSafety Commissioner Julie Inman Grant new powers to gather information and force companies to prove compliance with the new laws.

The Opposition voted against the bill, saying the changes were government overreach.

Communication Minister Anika Wells, however, said Labor stood with Australian families on the right side of history.

“Australian families will not forget the senators and members who sold them out for political points from the far right,” she said on Thursday (10 September).

“Today the Coalition voted against Labor’s bill to strengthen Australia’s social media minimum age laws.

“The modern Coalition has no shame, putting politics ahead of what Australians have demanded of their elected representatives.

“The Coalition chose to run a protection racket for big tech instead of backing Australian families and kids.”

Government overreach is also the broad reason the Coalition is using to flag its intention to oppose Labor’s next move on social media firms, which is to mandate an algorithm opt-out provision for all users.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said Labor’s draft Digital Duty of Care legislation allows too much ministerial discretion.

“That is not acceptable to the Coalition in its current form,” Mr Taylor said.

“Can I say that this is a government that cannot be trusted. This is a Minister who cannot be trusted … We should have free debate… It is incredibly important that we don’t have a minister controlling with a blank cheque what we see on the internet.”

Under Labor’s plan, online games, apps and AI chatbots will be required to protect under-18s from design features that have negative behavioural impacts, such as addictive features or those that can affect a young person’s self-esteem.

These include content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; hostile ideas about women and gender equality; pornography; glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; or causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.

Anthony Albanese has rejected any suggestion the bill could amount to political censorship.

“It’s not about censorship. It’s about giving people control themselves over what they see,” the Prime Minister said.

“We can emphatically rule that out. This is about basic safety standards online for online services and about the onus being on big tech to identify risks on their platform and to mitigate against those risks.”

The Coalition doesn’t quite see it that way.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan echoed Mr Taylor’s concerns, saying neither the PM nor Ms Wells could be trusted on the issue.

“This bill is not in place to protect the people of Australia. It is a bill to protect politicians,” Senator Canavan said.

“It’s a bill that will allow the government to dictate what you can say and see online. And we can never have that in place in this country.”

Shadow communications minister Sarah Henderson agreed there needs to be a debate about algorithms, but that it shouldn’t be wrapped up in the “Trojan horse” duty of care bill.

She said Labor was using the bill to censor Australians online and threaten free speech.

“The minister has given herself unfettered powers to make regulations in relation to any category of harm without parliamentary oversight,” Senator Henderson said.

The government intends to introduce the legislation proper to parliament in October and hopes to have it passed this year.

canberra.title: Coastal artist Tommy Novak reaches quarterfinals, plots special hometown tour
canberra.snippet: South Coast-born musician Tommy Novak has spent weeks winning hearts on national television, but now he’s preparing for a special t...
canberra.content:
Tommy Novak has teased his next performance on The Voice Australia, saying he’ll be playing the piano once again. Photo: Seven Network.

South Coast-born musician Tommy Novak has spent weeks winning hearts on national television, but now he’s preparing for a special trip to his hometown.

He has made it through to another stage of this year’s The Voice Australia, after surviving the knockout stage.

Tommy passed with an emotional cover of All By Myself, by American singer-songwriter Eric Carmen.

He was facing off against a small group of fellow artists to see who would move ahead to the quarterfinals.

“It was a pretty huge song that [coach] Richard [Marx] entrusted me with … It certainly wasn’t my first pick for a song to do,” he told Region.

“I certainly wasn’t expecting to get handed a song like that because it’s obviously one of those power ballads that it’s renowned for someone like Celine Dion.

“But what Richard asked me to do with that particular song was to actually take it back to its roots.”

His journey began when he wowed audiences – and the judges – with his cover of Landslide by Fleetwood Mac.

Since making it through his blind audition just a few weeks ago, he says a lot has changed.

“I think it certainly has had a huge influence on me, just in terms of my confidence to be myself on that stage and to wear my heart on my sleeve,” he said.

“I think it’s really helped me to get comfortable with expressing what I’m feeling through music – and performing is certainly part of that, right?”

In addition to competing on The Voice Australia, Tommy released his debut EP in July.

It’s “serendipitous” timing to have the EP release and the competition happening so near to each other, he said.

“I don’t think I could have necessarily planned for it … But I think it’s been really special for those two things to be happening at about the same time.”

Tommy began working on the EP, “Parallels”, after a separation.

“I turned to music to kind of help process my feelings … In the last 18 months, I spent a lot of time going back to writing.

“It’s something I’ve always loved, but wasn’t necessarily doing a lot of, and they formed what would be my EP.”

He’ll also be hosting a viewing party at the Republic Hotel in Sydney on Sunday (13 September) and performing for the crowd.

To celebrate the release of “Parallels”, Tommy is heading back to the coast later this month.

A few days after his show in Sydney, he’ll take to the stage at Batemans Bay’s The Starfish Deli on 18 September from 6:30 pm.

Tommy says he wants to give back during his visit home.

“While I’m down there, I’m going to go pay a visit to my school, Carroll College at Broulee … I really want to share with those kids. I suppose share with them perhaps what I don’t necessarily feel someone said to me.

“If someone had come to me when I was in school and said, ‘Hey, if this [music] is something that you really love and you’re really interested in it, there’s no reason why you shouldn’t pursue it’.”

While in his hometown, he will take to the stage as part of an extra-special concert.

“My sister, who has an intellectual disability, spends some time at a place called Yumaro … I’m going to go and spend some time at Yumaro, and perform a couple of songs for my sister and all of her friends there.

“I think that’ll be really special.”

When asked what he could tease about the upcoming The Voice Australia quarterfinals, Tommy wouldn’t reveal all his secrets.

“For the knockouts where I sang All by Myself, I played guitar … It was just me and an electric guitar, literally singing the lyrics all by myself,” he said.

“The thing that I can tell you is that I’m going to be jumping back on the piano on Sunday for the next song that I’m singing.”

The Voice Australia is airing on the Seven Network and on the 7plus streaming service. You can also follow Tommy’s upcoming gigs through his Facebook page and his website.

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: 15 places to see spectacular spring blooms across Canberra and southern NSW
canberra.snippet: When spring arrives, it’s tempting to start dreaming of plane tickets to Japan and picnics beneath the cherry blossoms. But before you fo...
canberra.content:
11 September 2026

Start the conversation

Tulip Top Gardens sits on the outskirts of Canberra and is a world away from Floriade in style and experience. Photo: Visit NSW.

When spring arrives, it’s tempting to start dreaming of plane tickets to Japan and picnics beneath the cherry blossoms. But before you fork out for a flight, why not take a look a little closer to home?

From sprawling tulip displays tended by a single family to flowing fields of fluorescent canola and orchards abundant with blossoms, it’s all here right on your doorstep.

Cowra Japanese Garden, Cowra

For a taste of Japan without the long-haul flight, Cowra is the place to begin. The five-hectare Japanese garden, which happens to be the largest in the Southern Hemisphere, explodes with cherry blossoms each September, and the blossoms aren’t alone; they are accompanied by magnolias, azaleas and beautifully hedged foliage that sets quite the scene.

The garden’s annual Sakura Matsuri festival, which takes place in late September, celebrates the season with Japanese food, music and cultural demonstrations, but you don’t need to attend the festival to see the blooms. The Cowra Japanese Garden is open daily from 8:30 am to 5 pm. Admission fees apply.

The canola fields of southern NSW cover the hillsides in golden flowers. Photo: Visit NSW.

Cowra canola country, Cowra

While the Japanese garden supplies Cowra’s pinks and whites, the countryside contributes great swathes of gold with its vast canola fields. Depending on the season, canola generally flowers from late August through September, with the locations changing each year according to crop rotations.

The safest way to find the best displays is to contact the Cowra Visitor Information Centre or simply jump in the car and start exploring the region. Remember that canola fields are working farms, so you’ll need to admire them from designated viewpoints and roadside stops.

Foxglove Gardens in Central Tilba offers accommodation if you want to make a weekend of it. Photo: Foxglove Gardens.

Foxglove Gardens, Central Tilba

Tucked beneath Gulaga at Central Tilba, Foxglove Gardens provides an escape to the English countryside. Spread across 1.2 hectares and filled with rambling paths, water features, garden rooms, roses, perennials and cottage flowers, you’ll feel like you’ve stepped straight into a Jane Austen novel.

There is no single mass-planted spectacle here; the pleasure is in wandering and discovering something new around each corner. Foxglove Gardens is generally open Wednesday to Sunday from 10 am to 5 pm, but check current hours before setting out. Turn your amble into a full weekend by booking a room at its onsite retreat.

Red Cow Farm offers a stunning Highlands escape. Photo: Visit NSW.

Red Cow Farm, Sutton Forest

Red Cow Farm is a garden for romantics and those who like to lose themselves in curated nature for a few hours. Spread across six acres in the historic village of Sutton Forest, it is divided into more than 20 garden rooms, including a cottage garden, monastery garden, beech walk, orchard and woodland.

Spring brings bulbs, blossom, clematis and rare perennials, with each space revealing itself gradually as you explore. Red Cow Farm is open daily from 10 am to 4 pm, with paid entry and the last admission at 3:30 pm.

Harper’s Mansion features one of the largest hedge mazes in Australia. Photo: National Trust.

Harper’s Mansion, Berrima

This grand Georgian House built in 1834 is surrounded by charming gardens that are an attraction in their own right. Linger among the heritage roses, cool-climate flowers, mature trees and orchards that all sit alongside one of the property’s most charming features, an extensive hedge maze.

The garden is especially lovely in late spring when the roses begin to bloom. Harper’s Mansion is open Saturday and Sunday from 11 am to 3 pm, with an admission fee applying.

Floriade is the Canberra region’s premier event of the year, attracting more than half a million visitors each year. Photo: Events ACT.

Floriade, Canberra

Canberra’s annual tulip festival, Floriade is the flower aficionado’s obvious spring choice, and for good reason. More than a million bulbs and annuals transform Commonwealth Park into a patterned patchwork of tulips, daffodils and carefully coordinated garden beds.

Over the years, Floriade has slowly morphed into a broader food and entertainment festival, but behind the concerts, markets and attractions is still one of Australia’s greatest flower displays. Entry to daytime Floriade is free; in 2026, the festival runs from 12 September to 11 October.

Cherry blossom trees in Nara Peace Park. Photo: John Lomnicki.

Nara Peace Park and Lennox Gardens, Canberra

If you’re already visiting Floriade, make time to cross the lake to Lennox Gardens and Nara Peace Park. The Japanese-themed garden’s cherry trees produce a delicate display of pink and white blossom, usually around late August and September.

It’s an easy win and an excellent place to spread out a picnic when Commonwealth Park is overrun with the tour bus crowds. Lennox Gardens and Nara Peace Park are free public spaces open daily, although the short blossom season means timing your visit carefully.

Canola in the Hilltops Shire is stunning in spring. Photo: Edwina Mason.

The Hilltops region’s canola country, Hilltops

The country around Boorowa, Galong, Harden-Murrumburrah and Young becomes one of the state’s great scenic drives when the canola is in bloom. Catch the golden fields in the morning light or in the late afternoon for the best views.

There is no admission fee to see the canola; this is a roadside attraction. Check with Hilltops Region tourism for current conditions, pull completely off the road before stopping, respect private property and don’t walk in the paddocks, and you’re in for a real treat.

The orchards around Young make for a great day out for eyes, body and tastebuds! Photo: Visit Hilltops Region.

Young’s cherry and stone fruit orchards, Young

Young is known as Australia’s cherry capital, but the spectacle begins well before the fruit arrives, as cherry trees, plums, peaches and nectarines come into bloom in the early spring, cloaking the region in clouds of white and pink blossom.

The orchards are private working properties rather than public parks, so visitors should seek out participating farms, organised blossom events or recommended roadside viewing points. Contact the Young Visitor Information Centre before travelling for current flowering conditions and places welcoming visitors.

Dave Purcell and family operate the Apple Thief Cider House which will embed you in orchard country. Photo: Apple Thief Cider House.

Batlow orchard country, Batlow

Batlow’s apple orchards announce the beginning of the growing season with a wash of pink and white blooms. At an elevation of around 750 metres, the town produces blossoms later than many lower-lying areas, usually around October.

A drive through the surrounding orchards provides the best overview, and a lunch stop at the Apple Thief Cider House is a must with its blossom-lined entry being quite the showstopper.

The orchards in the region are privately owned, so enjoy them from public roads or visit businesses that specifically advertise public access.

Kosciuszko offers high country wildflowers you’ll have to work for. Photo: Visit NSW.

Kosciuszko alpine wildflowers, Kosciuszko National Park

Australia’s high country offers a different and more subtle kind of floral experience. Once the snow begins to retreat, the alpine landscape is dotted with snow daisies, yellow billy buttons, alpine sunrays, marsh marigolds and the delicate anemone buttercup, which is found only in Kosciuszko National Park.

The timing of blooms is seasonally dependent, and this winter has been unseasonably warm, so think of this as a late spring and into summer destination with the best displays frequently extending into December and January. Popular routes to see the wild flowers include the Kosciuszko Walk from Thredbo and the Summit Walk from Charlotte Pass. Check NSW National Parks for track conditions, snow cover and park entry fees before visiting.

Tulip Top Gardens offers all the colour of Floriade in a far more intimate setting. Photo: Visit NSW.

Tulip Top Gardens, Sutton

Just north of Canberra, Tulip Top Gardens is an impressive private garden created and maintained by the Rhodin family, and it stands as a testament to what one family can achieve. Thousands of tulips and other spring bulbs flow beneath mature blossom trees, creating a far more intimate and enclosed experience than nearby Floriade.

Tulip Top Gardens opens daily from 12 September to 11 October, with paid entry at the gate.

You might spot more than just beautiful flowers at Corbett Gardens this time of year. Photo: @tuliptimeflowerfestival.

Tulip Time, Corbett Gardens, Bowral

Bowral has celebrated spring with tulips for more than six decades. During Tulip Time, Corbett Gardens is filled with tens of thousands of tulips and annuals, while smaller floral displays spill into public spaces across the town.

It’s also an excuse to explore the Southern Highlands at its most colourful, when blossom trees and cool-climate gardens are at their best across the region. Tulip Time runs from 11 September to 5 October in 2026, with tickets required for Corbett Gardens.

There’s plenty more to see at Fitzroy Falls than just the falls themselves, and the walking trails prove just that! Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Fitzroy Falls wildflower walks, Fitzroy Falls

Not every spring display needs a gardener, and the East Rim and Wildflower walking tracks at Fitzroy Falls offer a place to see nature do its thing without human interference. As you pass through heathlands, grassy woodlands and eucalypt forests, native flowers emerge among the sandstone, and sweeping views of the Southern Highlands are a reminder of the wonders on our doorstep.

The walk is about 6.7 kilometres return and takes two to three hours, although shorter sections can be enjoyed. The tracks are open year-round, subject to park conditions, and parking fees apply at Fitzroy Falls Visitor Centre.

Mayfield Garden sits in the Central Tablelands, with gardens spread across 65 hectares making it worth the drive. Photo: Visit NSW.

Mayfield Garden, Oberon

A little further afield in the Central Tablelands but definitely worth the drive is Mayfield Garden, which unfolds on a grand scale across 65 hectares.

Bringing together flowering trees, bulbs, rhododendrons, water features, formal garden rooms and one of the Southern Hemisphere’s largest hedge mazes, the established gardens are a true delight.

Allow several hours to explore the garden’s pathways, bridges, cascades and hidden corners. Mayfield Garden is open daily from 9 am to 4:30 pm, with the last entry at 3 pm and admission fees applying.

Original Article published by Tenele Conway on About Regional.

australia.title: One flight cancelled every three days due to staff shortages – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast ‘Profound’ increase in death rate for welfare recipi...
australia.content:
One flight cancelled every three days across Australia due to staff shortages

Luca Ittimani

Worker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year, Airservices Australia has told a Senate hearing.

The government agency’s deputy CEO, Peter Curran, said Australia’s airports recorded 2,536 cancellations over the year to 31 August, of which 121 were attributed to Airservices. Sydney accounted for 103 of those.

Just this morning, the troubled airport recorded 14 inbound cancellations and more outbound cancellations, after some overnight staff were unavailable, Curran said. Airservices and airlines manage the shortage by delaying or cancelling flights.

Curran said Sydney had grown and now needed a team of 41 air traffic controllers, spread across the roster. It has 49 employed but eight are unavailable at the moment. Curran said:

When we have a bit of short-term sickness or unavailability, like we had last night, it makes it very difficult to recover.

Curran said retired staff had been asked to come back to work but some of them were “simply not interested”. He said there were about 1,100 air traffic controllers working across Australia and 91 would join in the coming year.

With more recruitment, Curran said Airservices would be able to enough on-call staff to cover two absences a day by March 2027.

It’s not an ironclad model, but it certainly reduces the likelihood of the sorts of issues that we’re having today.
