What we learned – Friday 11 September

That’s a wrap on another eventful week in the news cycle.

Before we let you go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • Anthony Albanese has marked 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks in the US. Ten Australians were among 2,977 people killed in the terrorist attacks in New York, Washington DC and Pennsylvania – “lives tragically cut short far from home”.

  • The saga surrounding the One Nation cartoon labelling Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie a “traitor” continues as Pauline Hanson doubled down despite growing condemnation from all sides of parliament. Hastie said Barnaby Joyce had reached out to him with an explanation and apology, which he accepted.

  • The Victoria premier, Ben Carroll, joined in on the hype around the NFL game at the MCG this morning, calling it an exciting and historic day for the state.

  • Australia’s domestic spy agency said it has foiled 16 terrorist threats in the nine months since the Bondi attack, including an antisemitic attack.

  • Worker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year, Airservices Australia has told a Senate hearing.

That’s for sticking around, have a lovely weekend!

Roxanne Tickle welcomes rejection of Giggle’s appeal in landmark transgender discrimination case

The transgender woman at the centre of a successful discrimination case has welcomed the High Court’s rejection of an attempted appeal.

The High Court refused, with costs, an appeal by the women-only app Giggle against a Full Federal Court ruling in May. The ruling upheld a landmark decision that the app and its founder, Sall Grover, unlawfully discriminated against Roxanne Tickle after she was denied access to the platform.

In a statement, Tickle said:

It’s been nearly 5 years since I lodged my discrimination complaint. It’s been a relentlessly exhausting time, both physically and emotionally, for me and many others.

I hope that yesterday’s High Court special leave refusal provides clarity to the protections in law for transgender and gender diverse people in Australia, and perhaps provides a beacon of light to the rest of the world.

I wish my trans and gender diverse siblings, as well as their loved ones, much hope and love for their collective futures. May we all learn that just being different is not grounds for you to be ridiculed, attacked, feared or hated, but that instead you are providing a little something extra to the world. Life is not easy. Let’s all be kinder to each other and we might all enjoy it a little more.

Read the full story here:

Erin Patterson should receive peer counselling, prisoner rights group says

Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson is being kept in near constant isolation, leaving her frightened and at risk of psychological decline, AAP reports.

A prisoner rights group is advocating on the triple murderer’s behalf for her to receive peer counselling to improve her mental wellbeing at no cost to the state.

Patterson’s current conditions at the Dame Phyllis Frost centre, west of Melbourne, involve being confined to a cell for a minimum of 22 hours a day and having approved contact with just one other prisoner through a wire mesh during limited yard time.

Advocacy group Justice Action has called the treatment tantamount to torture, invoking United Nations rules named after Nelson Mandela which say a person should not spend more that 15 consecutive days in solitary confinement.

The group is yet to be allowed direct contact with Patterson, but says information from other prisoners in the same unit suggests she is in a poor mental state.

Justice Action co-ordinator Brett Collins, who is a former inmate, said Patterson was entitled to be treated like any other prisoner and to serve her time constructively. He told AAP on Friday:

She’s a frightened woman, understandably so.

She’s actually been now isolated for such a long time, and she’s already had those disorders before she before she was convicted, so now we’ve heard she’s unused to people being around her.

That’s the sort of behaviour that causes causes permanent damages. It’s torture, actually.

Justice Action is proposing Patterson be permitted a trained peer support mentor to help address and mitigate the psychiatric risks, which it would offer at no cost to taxpayers.

Major fire breaks out at building in Sydney’s north-west

Authorities are investigating the cause of a major building fire in Sydney’s north-west.

Emergency services responded to reports of the blaze on Loftus Street in Riverstone at around 1.35pm.

Fire and Rescue NSW said about 40 firefighters and 12 trucks remained at the scene. The fire has since been contained to the building where it started.

Four people were assessed at the scene, but none were taken to hospital.

Fire and Rescue NSW said the cause of the fire was under investigation.

Achol Arok

Hello! I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of afternoon’s news.

Nick Visser

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take the blog from here. Take care!

ATO employee charged after allegedly disclosing information to organised crime associates

An Australian Taxation Office employee has been charged with corruption-related offences by the AFP and other groups on allegations the man disclosed information obtained in his work to organised crime associates.

The AFP said today the Gold Coast man, 32, had been charged overnight with two counts of unlawfully disclosing information by a commonwealth officer. The offence carries a maximum penalty of two years in prison.

He is due in court later this month.

After a search warrant was carried out, the man was also charged with two counts of possession or control of child abuse material and 15 counts of using a carriage service for child abuse material. The maximum penalty for both offences is 15 years in prison.

Queensland’s credit rating downgraded for the first time in 17 years

Queensland has been dealt the first downgrade to its credit rating in 17 years, heaping more borrowing costs on to the state’s budget, AAP reports.

Credit agency S&P Global slapped a stable outlook on Queensland’s downgraded AA rating.

The loss of Queensland’s AA+ rating came on the same day NSW received an upgrade to its credit outlook. Queensland’s budget performance would remain “very weak” over the next two to three years compared to peers with a similar rating, S&P said on Friday.

The state’s historically large infrastructure program ahead of the 2032 Olympics and forecast deficits contrasted with previous expectations for sound surpluses from 2028, it said in a report.

The state could also expect lower stamp duty revenues after property tax changes in the federal budget exacerbated a deepening housing downturn, S&P said.

One flight cancelled every three days across Australia due to staff shortages

Luca Ittimani

Worker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year, Airservices Australia has told a Senate hearing.

The government agency’s deputy CEO, Peter Curran, said Australia’s airports recorded 2,536 cancellations over the year to 31 August, of which 121 were attributed to Airservices. Sydney accounted for 103 of those.

Just this morning, the troubled airport recorded 14 inbound cancellations and more outbound cancellations, after some overnight staff were unavailable, Curran said. Airservices and airlines manage the shortage by delaying or cancelling flights.

Curran said Sydney had grown and now needed a team of 41 air traffic controllers, spread across the roster. It has 49 employed but eight are unavailable at the moment. Curran said:

When we have a bit of short-term sickness or unavailability, like we had last night, it makes it very difficult to recover.

Curran said retired staff had been asked to come back to work but some of them were “simply not interested”. He said there were about 1,100 air traffic controllers working across Australia and 91 would join in the coming year.

With more recruitment, Curran said Airservices would be able to enough on-call staff to cover two absences a day by March 2027.

It’s not an ironclad model, but it certainly reduces the likelihood of the sorts of issues that we’re having today.

49ers rout Rams 27-7 in NFL clash at the MCG

Mike Evans, Demarcus Robinson and Deebo Samuel caught touchdown passes from quarterback Brock Purdy, and the San Francisco 49ers routed the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 Friday in the first NFL regular-season game in Australia.

Purdy passed for 205 yards against the Rams’ ineffective defense at the Melbourne Cricket Ground in front of 100,021 fans, the seventh-largest regular season crowd in NFL history.

Australia’s sporting capital reveled in its first real taste of American football – and in a dominant win by the 49ers, who had already won many Aussies’ affection by travelling to Melbourne a week earlier than the Rams, who only boomeranged in on Thursday morning.

Read more here:

NFL stars, cheerleaders and the Jonas Brothers as American football comes to Melbourne

About 100,000 fans filled the MCG for the historic NFL regular-season clash between the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne.

Die-hard supporters and interested spectators came from all corners to see American football’s cultural exchange, which included cheerleaders before the match and a Jonas Brothers show at half-time.

Take a look at some below:

Australian share market veering towards worst week since US-Iran war began

The Australian share market is barreling toward its worst week since the US-Iran war began, as surging oil prices pressure bond yields and squeeze central banks to hike borrowing costs.

The benchmark S&P/ASX200 index fell 112.2 points by midday on Friday, to be down 1.27% as the broader All Ordinaries tumbled 120 points, or 1.33%.

The top-200 is on track for a 3.2% slump since Monday and its worst week since early March’s 3.8% plunge, when US-led strikes killed Iran’s supreme leader and triggered a broader regional conflict.

The Australian dollar was buying 71.56 US cents, down from 72.16 US cents on Thursday at 5pm.

australia.title: Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’
australia.snippet: Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise Follow our...
australia.content:
Fuel prices are on track to climb a further 20-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, after the escalating Middle East conflict pushed the global oil price to its highest since mid-May.

As investors dumped stocks and bonds in an increasingly febrile environment, Donald Trump’s promise to give every US adult citizen a US$5,000 “dividend” after the November midterms if Republicans win added to alarm around the parlous state of the country’s finances.

Investors pushed US bond yields towards 5% for the first time since 2007 as the prospect of higher energy costs firmed up expectations that the US Federal Reserve would need to hike rates again.

That dragged Australia’s 10-year rate up to 5.38% and to fresh 15-year highs.

The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed towards US$110 a barrel, before settling at above US$108 in late Friday trade.

Steve Miller, an investment strategist at fund manager GSFM, said bonds were reacting to a “deadly cocktail” of high oil prices, American fiscal irresponsibility, and worries around the independence of the Fed.

“The $5,000 promise is a great example of Trump’s unwillingness to tackle the deficit, and even to make it worse for short-term political expediency. No wonder bond markets are sketchy,” Miller said.

Tai Hui, chief market strategist for Asia-Pacific at JP Morgan Asset Management, said rising long-term borrowing rates would normally undermine stock valuations, as investors rethink the relative trade-off between the riskier sharemarket and climbing yields on safe bonds.

Evidence of this was clear on the ASX this week, where the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index was on track to end the week down 3% and below the level it was this time last year.

But Hui said ongoing optimism about the state of the global economy and, especially, the titanic boom in artificial intelligence investment was providing a tailwind for sharemarkets around the world, and especially on Wall Street.

Since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran at the end of February, the US benchmark S&P 500 sharemarket index is up about 10%, against a 5% fall for the ASX 200.

But the Hong Kong-based Hui said the increasingly debated question among investors was at what point the steady march higher in yields begins to drive a broader and deeper switch out of stocks and into bonds.

“We are approaching a crossroad,” he said.

As economists warned of a new post-Covid era of structurally higher interest rates, financial markets upped their bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia would deliver a fourth rate hike on 29 September, pricing in an 80% chance.

Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said the RBA would have to respond to recent evidence that inflationary pressures were not easing as hoped, even as the economy proved resilient.

“I think they [the RBA] will go in September,” Kearns said.

The former top RBA official said the central bank’s inflation-fighting credentials were increasingly at stake.

“They need to get inflation to 2.5%, and that’s not forecast to happen until early 2028; that then becomes almost a seven-year inflationary episode.”

The prospect of higher mortgage costs comes as Vivek Dhar, CBA’s head of commodities research, warned that diesel prices could climb by 10-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, from over $2.50 per litre today.

Unleaded petrol prices could push from about $2.10 a litre in major east coast cities to about $2.30 over the next couple of weeks, according to a rough rule of thumb that says every US$1 increase in the crude oil benchmark translates to a 10c increase at the pump.

Dhar, who is based in Singapore, said meetings with energy producers and traders on the sidelines of a major energy conference over recent days revealed a deep sense of uncertainty about how the next six to 12 months will play out.

Dhar said he expected Brent crude to swing between US$70 and US$100 a barrel for the foreseeable future, until eventually the world becomes comfortable with the supply workarounds to a restricted strait of Hormuz.

But the more pressing worries were around the supply of refined products, particularly diesel.

“Everyone pays attention to oil, but it’s the refined product that hits the economy and feeds through to inflation. And that is what everyone is worried about, because there isn’t any workaround; we just need disruptions to stop.”

australia.title: NSW police settle trespass case after visiting Indigenous children’s home 150 times in 20 months
australia.snippet: Trespass case launched by two mothers settled after officers often went to families’ houses between midnight and 4am Follow our Australia...
australia.content:
Two Indigenous mothers have settled a trespass case against New South Wales police, after officers turned up at one of their homes 150 times in 20 months to conduct bail checks on her sons.

The case, which was launched against NSW police in April 2024, was settled on confidential terms three weeks before it was to go to trial in the supreme court.

One of the complainants, a single mum who uses the pseudonym Megan for privacy, has two sons, who were on bail from the ages of 11 and 13 after being found as passengers in a stolen car.

Police attended her home in regional NSW more than 150 times over 20 months, with many of the visits taking place between midnight and 4am.

NSW legislation allows courts to authorise police to attend a private residence to check that someone is complying with their bail conditions.

But the Justice and Equity Centre, representing Megan in court, argued that many of the bail checks were done without court authorisation, which amounted to trespass.

Megan said the visits often involved police banging on doors, shining torches through the windows and letting themselves in through the back gate in the middle of the night.

She said the visits were scary and stressful for her family and resulted in her kids missing school because of exhaustion.

‘‘My eldest is driving around with his head held high now, knowing police can’t just randomly pull him over,’’ Megan said.

‘‘But I know he’s still shaking in fear about what they could do.

‘‘They’ve already done the damage, and it will take a lot for my boys to start trusting police again.”

The other complainant, a single mum of three who uses the pseudonym Joanne, said police visited her western Sydney home to do bail checks on her son more than 90 times in 18 months.

She said in the space of a few hours, police conducted three such checks.

“The checks often happened on school nights, which meant my youngest daughter was too tired to go to school in the morning,” she said.

NSW police said the officers were acting lawfully when they conducted the bail compliance checks.

A police spokesperson said such checks were an important tool for keeping the public safe and managing risks associated with letting people out of jail during an ongoing court process.

But a report from the state’s Law Enforcement Conduct Commission, released in 2025, found police were stretching their authority and powers by relying on a weak legal principle to conduct bail compliance checks without court authorisation.

The mothers’ solicitor, Kate Sinclair, said it was immensely brave for her clients to bring the case against the force.

‘‘They did it for their families and their communities and we respect their courage,’’ she said.

Megan and her sons have separately taken NSW police to the federal court for racial discrimination, arguing that the boys were targeted because they are Aboriginal.

That case is ongoing.

australia.title: In need of the warm and fuzzies? Joyous exhibition celebrates 70 years of the Muppets and the genius of Jim Henson
australia.snippet: Make, Believe, Magic show at Goma stars Elmo, Big Bird and the massive Mr Snuffleupagus – and gives visitors the chance to try their hand...
australia.content:
Make, Believe, Magic show at Goma stars Elmo, Big Bird and the massive Mr Snuffleupagus – and gives visitors the chance to try their hand at puppeteering

It’s said that celebrities are often shorter than you might expect when you encounter them in person. The opposite is true of the Muppets.

“That’s the quote of this show,” says Amanda Slack-Smith, curator at Queensland’s Gallery of Modern Art (Goma), where “Oh, it’s bigger than I thought it would be!” has become a catchcry among the Goma crew installing Make, Believe, Magic: The Worlds of the Jim Henson Company.

As we stand in awe of Big Bird and Mr Snuffleupagus – those gentle giants of childhood naivety from Sesame Street – it’s easy to see why. And maybe it’s my imagination, or the transportive power of whimsy unleashed, but I swear Snuffy just winked at me.

Several years in the making, this joyous exhibition celebrates the unmatched genius of Jim Henson: writer, director, artist, puppeteer and creator of the Muppets. It features more than 500 objects – puppets, props, costumes, photos, sketches, storyboards and more – sourced from the Jim Henson Company’s extensive archive, plus several other US institutions.

Taking in the breadth of the company’s 70-year history, the exhibition charts not only Henson’s career, cut short by his unexpected death in 1990, but the body of work produced by his heirs, both literal and spiritual, who carry the torch for puppetry, animatronics and practical effects into the digital age.

Occupying Goma’s entire ground floor, the exhibition stretches over three realms, exploring the making, performance and possibilities of puppetry, respectively. As Slack-Smith guides me through the first rooms, it feels like, wherever you look, some fuzzy face returns your gaze.

Old pals like Grover and Elmo beam from their plinths, while lesser-known monsters and oddballs (for example, the creepy-cute cast of Jim Henson’s Turkey Hollow, a Thanksgiving special from 2015) also get their time out of the archive and into the spotlight.

A decent handful of these puppets have never been displayed before. “This is the only second time that Snuffy’s been out of the US,” Slack-Smith says. When I ask how a sir of Snuffy’s length – 13 feet from trunk to tail – is transported from New York to Brisbane, she grins: “It’s a mystery.”

Another hulking highlight shipped across the Pacific is Fraggle Rock itself. The subterranean set of Fraggle Rock: Back to the Rock – the 2022 reboot of Henson’s original 1980s series – sprawls across one room. We stroll from Doc’s workshop to the Gorgs’ garden to the Fraggles’ cavernous Great Hall, where every nook and cranny is seasoned with details from both iterations of the show.

The Goma press release describes the exhibition as “immersive”, a term I’d assumed was marketing hyperbole. But as I follow Slack-Smith into Boober’s Cave, the Fraggles’ clean laundry hanging overhead, I genuinely feel the temperature drop.

More importantly, this isn’t just a site for fan service and photo opps. It’s designed as a working set, reconstructed at the elevated height screen puppetry requires, with live feeds running to interactive vision mixers, and a platform where patrons can try their hand at the demanding craft.

“It’s meant to feel like everyone’s gone to lunch and you get to have a bit of a play,” Slack-Smith says, leading me behind the scenes, literally, to the back of Fraggle Rock. “You can actually see how they build the sets. Some of it’s hand-carved, some of it’s cast. You can see where it’s had a life, because it’s been used on multiple seasons and specials.” She points to some G-rated graffiti – “Mokey for President!” – scrawled by puppeteers on the back of the set.

“Puppeteering is an ancient art form,” the curator continues as we head into the next room. “It’s used for storytelling, and there’s something about mediating through a third party that means you get to have conversations that are hard and tough. But you get to relax into it. Puppeteering as an art form is integral to how we move through life.”

Moving away from the hand and rod puppetry of the Muppets, the exhibition also explores the animatronic innovations of Jim Henson’s Creature Shop, particularly in feature films. Henson’s own works, like The Dark Crystal (1982) and Labyrinth (1986), are well represented, alongside titles to which the company has contributed all manner of lifelike animalia. I spy Duchess the cat from Babe (1995) and a pigeon from The Producers (2005). “Thirty-five years since Jim’s passing,” Slack-Smith says, “they’re still this really dynamic, vibrant company doing incredible work.”

Some of the animatronic specimens have been stripped back to expose wires, gears, levers and eyeballs; the sense of the uncanny can’t be ignored (in abject contrast to the warm-fuzzy familiarity of Bert and Ernie). But in our current era of CGI screenscapes – increasingly diluted by AI corner-cutting – it’s marvellous to look upon physical, material, tangible evidence of screen culture.

“We’re living in a time when everything’s slipping and sliding,” Slack-Smith says. “You feel like you’re in an ocean, the sand’s coming out from under your feet, and you’re just trying to work out what’s real.”

This renders Make, Believe, Magic much more than a simple nostalgia trip. It’s a timely reminder that the most affecting art is made not by algorithm or prompt, but by human hand and heart.

Covering seven decades of the Jim Henson Company’s output, the exhibition is definitely comprehensive. Unless your favourite Muppet is Angus McGonagle (the Argyle Gargoyle who gargles Gershwin gorgeously), you’re highly likely to find them here – with a few exceptions.

Some visitors may note the conspicuous absence of headlining Muppets including Fozzie Bear, Gonzo the Great, and that eternal diva Miss Piggy. Since 2004, those characters have been owned by the Walt Disney Company, not the Jim Henson Company. Works by the latter are the clear curatorial focus here, though some select puppets – including the world’s most famous frog – have made their way over from the House of Mouse.

At the time of my visit, the Goma crew is busy putting the finishing touches on the show. The visiting puppet wranglers from Henson have worked their magic posing the characters and flown back to the US (boy, are their arms tired). Some of the lights are yet to be lit (or, rather, dimmed); the music is a symphony of drills, hammers and cherrypickers.

But controlled chaos is the Muppet way: an eclectic team pitching in to get the curtain up on time. Slack-Smith, the Kermit of the crew, seems unfazed. “I’ve got a theatre background. So, for me, working with the crew and putting this together is fun, when you’re running towards one creative outcome.”

And despite the occasional ladder and drop sheet, her vision is clear: “I want people to have a better understanding of puppeteering, of character and performance – but also to embrace the joy.”

  • Make, Believe, Magic: The Worlds of the Jim Henson Company is open until 18 April 2027

australia.title: Hastie accepts apology from Joyce over ‘traitor’ cartoon as Hanson doubles down and tells critics to ‘chill’
australia.snippet: A split emerges in One Nation over the video, with Barnaby Joyce offering an apology as Pauline Hanson continues to refuse to take it dow...
australia.content:
Andrew Hastie has accepted an apology from his former colleague Barnaby Joyce over a One Nation cartoon video labelling the former SAS captain a traitor but reiterated that he believed Pauline Hanson was a “lying coward”.

The apology has revealed a split between Joyce and his leader, as Hanson instead appeared to double down on the controversial animation on social media, thanking Hastie for drawing attention to the video posted more than one month ago and saying critics should “take a chill pill”.

Hastie had called on Hanson and One Nation to take ownership of the cartoon or remove it from social media, after the One Nation leader said she personally had not called the Liberal frontbencher a traitor.

The One Nation video posted to social media in late July depicts Hastie as a pitiful and paranoid opposition leader manipulated by Anthony Albanese into taking on One Nation.

It also refers to him being a traitor after he gave evidence against the Victoria Cross-winner Ben Roberts-Smith in his failed defamation trial.

Joyce quickly distanced himself from the video on Wednesday, saying he was not aware of it. He later told the press he had reached out to Hastie.

On Friday Hastie told Guardian Australia he accepted Joyce’s explanation.

“Barnaby Joyce has reached out to me and explained that he didn’t know about the cartoon that called me a traitor eight times,” Hastie said. “I accept his explanation.

“I called him a lying coward because I thought he was protecting Pauline Hanson. I now know that she is the only lying coward.”

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Hastie has accused Hanson of being “weak” and having a “glass jaw” and said the video not only insults him but all veterans, including others who gave evidence at the defamation trial.

Hanson has refused to apologise or pull down the video and has taken aim at critics including Jacqui Lambie, who backed Hastie and called the One Nation leader an “angry little woman”.

She posted a photo of Lambie on X and wrote: “I think everyone needs to take a chill pill.” The video remained pinned to the top of her X account on Friday.

Joyce would not weigh into whether the video should be taken down, telling News24 on Thursday night it was “beyond my pay grade”.

“I’m not responsible for putting the cartoons up and I’m not responsible for taking them down,” he MP said. “So, you know, it’s an odd discussion for me.

“If I believe a person’s hurt and I listen to it and I think, no, that’s fair enough, you’re not a traitor, therefore if you feel hurt by that because you think it’s too close to the bone, even though it’s a cartoon, I’m not making excuses because it’s a cartoon, but it wasn’t actually said by anybody in One Nation to him then nonetheless, it should be apologised for, so I apologise.”

But the One Nation senator Sean Bell said it was a “shame” Hastie had decided to make the issue about himself.

“I don’t think the party has anything to apologise for,” he told News24. “I think people should go and watch the cartoon, because I think, in it, there’s a lot of very insightful things, because it’s not just about Mr Hastie, it’s about the Liberal party as a whole. It’s about the Labor party and some of the tricks they use.

“Mr Hastie’s has been looking to have a fight and a conflict with One Nation for a long, long time.”

Senior Liberals, Lambie, the RSL and the Greens have all criticised the video, and pushed for it to be taken down.

On Friday the defence minister and deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, said the use of the word traitor was “tasteless”.

“Andrew Hastie is definitely not a traitor,” he told ABC radio. “I know him well and I’ve said this publicly. I very much honour the service that Andrew Hastie has given to our country, wearing our nation’s uniform. I think to use that word in respect of a veteran is extremely tasteless.

“No one should be using that word in respect of any veteran and in respect of Andrew.”

world.title: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide
world.snippet: Her Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globally Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against ...
world.content:
Frontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than 230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.

The launch of the fund comes as women’s rights are increasingly under attack and donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.

The United Nations has set a goal of elimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.

Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.

The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.

The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.

Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up the Ifrah Foundation to end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”

UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.

Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.

“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.

Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.

In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.

The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering a constitutional challenge to the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the new Child Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.

Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.

“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”

She added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”

Gibbs, who attended a Justice for Girls global gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.

“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.

“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”

FGM is the partial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.

A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately 44,000 deaths each year in the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.

world.title: Secret son revelation ignites bitter succession dispute in Ugandan kingdom
world.snippet: Family of late King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV reject committee’s choice of cousin and TV presenter as new monarch A traditional ...
world.content:
A traditional Ugandan kingdom has become engulfed in a bitter succession dispute after the family of a king who recently died rejected the selection of a television news anchor as his successor.

King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who became the world’s youngest reigning monarch when he took the throne in the kingdom of Tooro in 1995 at the age of three, died on 27 August in the US, where he was receiving cancer treatment.

On Wednesday, the royal clan’s succession committee announced it had chosen Oyo’s cousin Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at the public broadcaster UBC, as crown prince.

However, at a press conference held later the same day, Oyo’s sister, Princess Ruth Nsemere Komuntale, said that according to her brother’s will, a son whose existence had not been publicly known until his death should succeed him.

The kingdom’s ‌spokesperson shared a section of the document, which says: “I hereby declare and direct that if, at the date of my death, I am survived by a son lawfully recognised as my biological son, I appoint him as my heir to the throne of the kingdom of Tooro.”

In a statement on Thursday, Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Akiiki, denounced a “self-appointed group of clan members” who had selected a new king despite having had the will read to them hours earlier.

She also claimed that the royal family had been put under house arrest. Troops had “removed the royal guards without notice, and ... were deployed around the palace,” she said. “We cannot leave or receive people freely.”

Oyo was unmarried and was not known to have any children. The Tooro kingdom’s prime minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, revealed the existence of a son in a social media post on 27 August when announcing Oyo’s death.

“His majesty leaves behind a prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro kingdom,” he said.

Another contender had been Prince George Desmond-Kamurasi, who plays for the London amateur football club South East Dons. According to the committee, the goalkeeper had declined the offer of the throne because of his other responsibilities.

The Tooro king is selected by a succession committee appointed by the royal clan. A committee member told the local NTV station that a royal child must be officially introduced to elders in order to be considered for leadership.

Andrew Mwenda, ⁠a prominent Ugandan journalist and relative of the royal family, wrote on X on Thursday that Oyo’s ​family had not been able to produce a photo ​of the purported son, and declined to disclose ​details about the family of the boy’s mother. He added that, in Tooro, a king’s son could only succeed ​him if he were born to ‌a queen officially married ​to the king.

The prime minister ​called for restraint on Thursday. “There will be time to examine the will, to hear those advancing a different position, and to consider our customs, the applicable law and the proper institutions through which succession should be determined,” he said in a social media post.

“That process should take place calmly and credibly, not through competing announcements, confrontation, or attempts to establish facts on the ground while our king still awaits burial.”

Edward, a popular TV news presenter, is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of the former king George David Rukidi III.

Oyo, who was crowned after his father’s death, will be buried on Saturday at the Karambi royal tombs in the kingdom’s capital of Fort Portal in western Uganda.

Uganda has several ancient kingdoms that lack formal sovereignty, but whose leaders are revered as symbols of tradition and wield vast social influence. Tooro is one of five that are recognised by the government. Their monarchs have no political authority and are legally barred from engaging in partisan politics.

In 1967 Uganda’s then president, Milton Obote, abolished the kingdoms, saying he wanted to unify the country. They were restored by the current president, Yoweri Museveni, in 1993.

The Tooro are the latest African royal family to become mired in a succession dispute. King Misuzulu Sinqobile kaZwelithini, the reigning king of the Zulu people in South Africa, waited 15 months for his coronation after the death of his father because of a bitter feud involving accusations of forgery and poisoning.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

world.title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief
world.snippet: Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’ Uganda is withdrawing f...
world.content:
Uganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’s Invictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.

Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”

The timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.

When asked by the Times about what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”

The news, first reported by the Uganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.

At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.

The Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.”

The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.

The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”.

Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threats against Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.

The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.

world.title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds
world.snippet: Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems Babies born to mother...
world.content:
Babies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.

Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.

More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-Saharan Africa and south Asia.

Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town in South Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.

On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.

Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.

“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.

The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.

Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.

“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”

The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.

The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.

The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.

The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.

While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress has stagnated over the past two decades.

“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.

The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.

It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.

Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”

world.title: Hijacking pirates exploit regional chaos to return to seas off Somalia
world.snippet: US-Israel war on Iran and political instability in Somalia lead to pirates targeting cargo ships off Horn of Africa The scourge of Somali...
world.content:
The scourge of Somali piracy targeting cargo ships and smaller dhows off the Horn of Africa has returned to levels not seen in a decade, driven by a convergence of factors including disruptions to the shipping industry caused by the US-Israeli war against Iran and a resurgence of political instability in Somalia.

Since late April there have been eight hijackings by Somali pirates, including two within the space of a fortnight in August: one targeting an oil tanker with ties to Iran, the other a Cameroon-flagged vessel, the Lutuf, carrying military equipment for Turkey.

Over a seven-year period from 2005 there were more than 1,000 attacks on vessels in the waters off Somalia, which has mainland Africa’s longest coastline. Thousands of crew members were taken hostage, netting $400m (£296m) in ransom payments for the piracy network’s financiers, the low-level “foot-soldier” pirates and the communities who provided them with goods and services. The attacks only petered out after a multinational anti-piracy force was deployed.

The hijacking of the Lutuf was the most high-profile of the recent incidents. Turkey has been expanding its influence in Somalia after an agreement signed in 2024 to build up its navy, and the Lutuf’s release two weeks after its capture involved a joint Turkish-Somali operation that resulted in the destruction of four pirate vessels.

However, local officials including Mohamed Mubarak, the head of the Puntland security coordination office, have said that a $2.5m (£1.85m) ransom was also paid, prompting warnings that such payments risked encouraging similar incidents.

In a comment for the Center for Maritime Security in July, Matthew Reisener, the thinktank’s national security adviser, warned that naval campaigns by Iran in the strait of Hormuz and Iran’s Houthi proxies in the Red Sea – launched in response to the US-Israel war on Iran – are allowing regional piracy “to once again thrive”.

He wrote: “Not only have the global navies that once combatted piracy off the Horn of Africa diverted their resources to counter the threats against ships in these critical waterways, but these conflicts have also drawn maritime traffic closer to Somalia’s coastline, creating openings for opportunistic pirates to target commercial ships.”

According to Reisener, about 70% of maritime traffic that passed through the Red Sea prior to the Houthis’ targeting of ships there is now being rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa.

A report by the International Institute for Strategic Studies in May reached a similar conclusion: “The recent deterioration of maritime security followed a prolonged period of relative calm in the waters off the Somali coast, which resulted in the redeployment of international anti-piracy fleets and the relaxation of commercial risk-management practices. These factors – alongside the distraction posed by Houthi attacks in the Red Sea – have converged to create an opening that Somali pirates have been quick to exploit.”

Analysts also note that rising oil prices driven by the war have made oil cargoes a more valuable target.

Among the least developed countries in the world, Somalia has endured conflict and clan battles with no strong central government since the autocratic ruler Mohamed Siad Barre fell in 1991. Insufficient patrol vessels and an inability to regularly pay salaries to those involved in coastal patrols are among the reasons why Somalia has long-struggled to secure its coastline.

Piracy has historically thrived during periods of increasing instability and political, factional and regional competition. Observers say the recent rise in incidents has been exacerbated by a domestic and international focus on arms smuggling to Yemen by networks acting on behalf of Iran. Analysts suggest some of these networks have become increasingly associated with Somalia’s Islamist al-Shabaab group as it once again expands its territorial control in central and southern Somalia and seeks to build ties with the Houthis in Yemen.

Local officials interviewed by the Guardian described how in the recent spate of incidents, pirate groups have been using vessels they had already seized to attack and capture other vessels.

According to the officials, the Lutuf was approached as it sailed three nautical miles from Somali shores near the fishing town of Maraya by a previously hijacked cement carrier, the MV Sward, which had been repurposed as a pirate mothership. Eight gunmen from the Sward then boarded the Lutuf and were able to overpower the ship’s armed guards.

Officials say the recent attacks have also been marked by increased technological sophistication on the part of pirate groups, including the use of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service to facilitate the tracking of potential targets and for high-speed communications between pirates.

That reflects what Lloyd’s List has described as an increasingly “more capable and adaptive Somali piracy threat” that is already exposing vulnerabilities in carriers’ existing anti-piracy security measures.

In the weeks since the Lutuf ransom was paid, residents of Galkayo, a commercial hub in the north-central Mudug region, said money had started circulating through the local economy to a much greater degree than before. Consumption of the stimulant khat has reportedly increased, and greater numbers of expensive sports utility vehicles have been seen on the roads.

During the previous piracy boom, increased flows of money through the economies of coastal communities and places like Galkayo had profound societal impacts, including an expansion of alcohol and drug use and prostitution.

Perhaps foreshadowing the regime of tougher measures that may be required to counter the growing piracy threat, the Lutuf was only released after a series of drone attacks on the pirate groups involved in the seizure, both at sea and on land. The dead included nine armed men who were killed by a missile fired from a Turkish drone as they prepared boats to join the gunmen onboard the Lutuf.

The question now is whether the growing threat can be countered.

Writing in The Conversation in May, the UK-based academics Anja Shortland and Federico Varese, who studied Somalia’s piracy problem in 2014, were uncertain whether there was an international appetite or the capacity for the same sort of anti-piracy force deployed more than a decade ago.

“What happens next will depend on how the current hijacks proceed. Pirates rely on ransoms for reinvestment and to attract young men into their no-win-no-fee contracts. Fast and generous payments … may free the captive ships. But they will lead to escalating risks for everyone else.

“No state or alliance also currently has the will or capacity to run a naval mission on the scale seen in 2011 and 2012, when navies worldwide spent more than US$1bn annually on counter-piracy operations off Somalia.

“Although piracy manifests as a sea-based problem, it can only be solved on land.”
